explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The elder prays that Gaius will prosper and enjoy good health "…as your soul also prospers." So he's saying Gaius's soul is already prospering. Nice thing to pray over a friend.

Close, baker, but the text doesn't mention his household. The elder prays that Gaius will prosper and enjoy good health "…as your soul also prospers." So the thing already doing well is his soul. The rest is the prayer for the future.

Good guess, since prospering sounds like money talk. But this letter never mentions a business. The elder prays for Gaius to prosper and enjoy good health "…as your soul also prospers." The soul is the one already doing well.

explanations.answer: Hearing his children walk in the truth
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The elder says, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth." Nothing tops it for him. Not even a fresh tray of cookies, and I don't say that lightly.

explanations.answer: Seeing his churches grow in number
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The letter never talks about churches growing in number. The elder says, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth." His biggest joy is about how people walk, not how many there are.

explanations.answer: Hearing his letters were read aloud
explanations.explanation: Fun guess, baker, but the elder never says that. His words are, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth." It's about people living the truth, not about who read what. I'd love it if my recipes got read aloud, though.

That's it, baker. The elder says Gaius is faithful in what he does for the brothers, "…and especially since they are strangers to you." Helping people who are strangers to you takes something extra. Anybody can feed a friend.

explanations.answer: They are old friends of his
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. The text says the opposite. The elder says Gaius is faithful "…especially since they are strangers to you." He's helping people he doesn't even know.

I see why you'd go there, baker, but the text never says Gaius has little. The elder says he's faithful "…especially since they are strangers to you." The special part is that these brothers are strangers to him.

explanations.answer: In a manner worthy of God
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The elder says Gaius will do well to send them on their way "…in a manner worthy of God." The bar isn't a big show. It's the way God deserves. That's a high standard, higher than any of my cookie boxes.

explanations.answer: In a manner worthy of kings
explanations.explanation: Kings sound fancy, baker, but that's not in the text. The elder says Gaius will do well to send them on their way "…in a manner worthy of God." God is the measure here, not any king.

explanations.answer: In a manner pleasing to the church
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, baker, since the church comes up in the verse. But the elder's words are, "…in a manner worthy of God." The church heard about Gaius's love, and God is the standard for sending the brothers off.

True, baker. The elder says, "Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth." Supporting them puts you on the team. You don't have to be the one traveling to have a hand in the work.

Careful on this one, baker. The text says it plainly: "Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth." So the statement is true. Supporting them is how we become fellow workers.

Not this time, baker. The text says the opposite. The elder writes, "I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction." He wrote, and Diotrephes said no.

Yes, baker, false. The elder says Diotrephes, "…who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction." The letter went out, and Diotrephes wasn't taking it. Some folks just want the front of the line.

That's the word, baker. The elder says Diotrephes "…refuses to welcome the brothers…" These were traveling brothers, and the door stayed shut. I spent years in the back of a dark junk drawer before an angel called me out, so I think that stings.
Nope, baker. The word is "welcome." The elder says Diotrephes "…refuses to welcome the brothers…" It's about whether he'd take them in, not whether he'd stop by.

Good thinking, since the elder just mentioned instruction. But the word in the verse is "welcome." The elder says Diotrephes "…refuses to welcome the brothers…" Teaching isn't what he's turning down here.

explanations.answer: Forbids them and puts them out
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The elder says Diotrephes "…forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church." He didn't stop at saying no for himself. He blocked the others too, and that's heavy.

explanations.answer: Warns them but lets them go ahead
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The text says Diotrephes "…forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church." A warning would've been mild by comparison. He went further than that, and it's a heavy part of the letter.

explanations.answer: Asks the elder to settle it by letter
explanations.explanation: Hmm, baker, that's not in the text. It says Diotrephes "…forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church." Nothing there about a letter asking the elder to settle it. It's a heavy part of the letter.
Yes, baker. The elder says, "…do not imitate what is evil, but what is good." Then he adds, "The one who does good is of God…" Copy the good stuff. It's the best recipe going.
Not this one, baker. The elder says, "…do not imitate what is evil, but what is good." Popular isn't the measure. Plenty of popular things have burned a lot of people.
I see the logic, baker, but the word is "good." The elder says, "…do not imitate what is evil, but what is good." Safe is about staying out of trouble, and good is about what you actually do.

Not quite, baker. The elder says the opposite. Right after the good report on Demetrius, he writes, "We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true." So he adds his voice to everybody else's.

Right, baker, false. Demetrius has a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself. Then the elder adds, "We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true." He adds his voice to the rest.
True, baker. The elder ends with, "Greet each of our friends there by name." By name, not just a wave at the crowd. That's a warm way to close a letter.
Look again, baker. The last line says, "Greet each of our friends there by name." So the elder does ask Gaius to greet them, one by one. Names matter, and I'd say that's a good thing to remember.
